text: Notwithstanding the prestige often attached to a university degree, higher education today faces mounting scrutiny over whether it consistently delivers on its promises. Tuition has risen sharply in many countries, prompting some undergraduates to drop out before completing their credentials, while others graduate burdened with debt they will spend decades repaying. Nevertheless, few would dispute that rigorous scholarship remains indispensable to society; without academia's sustained investment in empirical research, groundbreaking discoveries in medicine, technology, and the social sciences would simply not occur. What is less widely understood, however, is how fragile the research process itself can be. A flawed methodology, an unrepresentative sample, or funding tied to a particular outcome can all skew results in ways that even a peer-reviewed publication does not always catch. Consequently, a growing number of scientists now delve into replication studies, attempting to reproduce earlier findings before accepting them as reliable. Were universities to prioritize replicable, transparent research over sheer volume of output, public trust in academic findings would likely improve. Meanwhile, students writing a dissertation are reminded, often repeatedly, to cite their sources meticulously; plagiarism, however unintentional, can undermine years of otherwise careful work.
